beats: Hook: 12 x 34 = ? The model answers eight times; only the answers a calculator agrees with (408) earn a reward. [line_grpo_card_board, line_rl_checker_box, line_dice_hand]

RL in one loop: an actor acts, the environment returns a reward and a new state, the actor updates its policy (the speaker's example: tic-tac-toe against the computer, no reward until the game ends; our analogy: a puppy and treats). [line_rl_tictactoe, line_rl_puppy_treat, line_dog_homework]

SFT vs RL: SFT copies a dataset people prepared offline; in RL the model writes its own answers online and the grade decides what it learns. [line_sft_copybook, line_rl_self_attempt, line_coder_storyteller]

RLHF: people pick the better of two answers, a reward model learns their taste, then RL (PPO) trains against that judge; costs: people in the loop, their bias, weak on math and code. [line_rlhf_raters, line_rlhf_judge_paddle, line_same_question]
RLVR: the judge is a few lines of code that only checks right or wrong (+1 / -1); no human labels. [line_rl_checker_box]

GRPO: sample a group of G answers per prompt (sampling makes them differ) and score each against its own group (relative advantage): 408 is pushed up, 56 is pushed down. [line_grpo_card_board, line_dice_hand, line_tally_pages]
What happened: in the R1 paper math scores rose sharply and the answers grew longer on their own (numbers: FACTS). [line_rl_longer_answers, line_long_ribbon, line_grow]

Where it works: anything with a checkable answer (math, code, agent tasks); RL takes a growing share of training compute (redraw slide 13 as two cakes, no brand). [line_rl_compute_cakes, line_gpu, line_servers]
Takeaway: if a program can check it, the model can practise it. [line_rl_self_attempt, line_rl_checker_box, line_burst]
